name: Цугцванг: взяття пішака
description:
In the past lessons, one player always had a passed pawn. In this lesson we are dealing with positions in which both players have a pawn. The idea is to conquer the other player's pawn through clever king play and opposition.


Losing a pawn does not necessarily mean losing the game. Again, clever use of opposition can keep the game a draw. Of course it depends on whether the other player's pawn has crossed the center line.

In examples 1 and 2 we see a similar situation, but with an important difference. In both cases black loses his/her pawn. In Example 1, this means the loss of the game. The white king ends up on the 6th row in front of its own pawn and we know from lesson 6 that this is a standard win. Having opposition no longer plays a role. In Example 2, all pieces are one row down and now black can make a draw. If white captures the pawn, black can move his/her king opposite the white one: opposition!

In example 3, black also loses his/her pawn, but he/she can choose where to lose the pawn. By losing the pawn on the 5th row, he/she can make a draw.

In Example 4, we see how white skillfully wins the pawn on the 6th row and thus achieves a winning position. With black to move, the position is a draw because he/she can then keep opposition (Example 5).

What do you have to do?

Capture the pawn and then bring your passed pawn to the other side.

Are you the defending party? Then keep a draw.

examples.text: If it is black's move, black must release the pawn. White can take advantage of this. By sticking to the black pawn with the king, black gets in zugzwang. White plays 1.Kd7. After 1...Kf8 2.Kxe6 Ke8 black does have opposition, but we know from lesson 6 that this does not save black here. With a pawn passed the center line and the king in front of its own pawn, white always wins: 3.Kd6 Kd8 4.e6 Ke8 5.e7 Kf7 6.Kd7 Kf6 7.e8Q.

Black to move loses the pawn. Nevertheless, this does not mean that the game is lost. Consider where black wants to place the king at the moment white captures the pawn on e5. If black then has opposition, they hold a draw. This is the case on square e7. We therefore move to a square adjacent to e7, so that after capturing on e5, black can put the king on e7.

1...Kf7 2.Kxe5 Ke7. Opposition! This is the first example from Lesson 5. White cannot make progress: 3.Kd5 Kd7 4.e5 Ke7 5.e6 Ke8 6.Kd6 Kd8 7.e7+ Ke8 8.Ke6 stalemate.

It's black to move. Tempting here is to cover the pawn with 1...Kf7?, but after 2.e5 (reserve tempo!) Black not only loses the pawn because of zugzwang, but moreover the pawn is lost in an unfortunate spot. In the first example we saw how black loses from this position.

1...e5 draws. After 2.Kxe5 Ke7 black has opposition. We saw the same position in example 2.

examples.text: White's move. In this position we work toward Example 1. White wants to reach square d6 with their king. This is not possible right away, so White takes a detour. White pushes the black king away slowly. 1.Kb6 Kd8. Black cannot prevent the white king from entering. 2.Kc6 Ke7 3.Kc7 (opposition!) 3...Ke8 and now the white king goes the other way than the black one and reaches the crucial square: 4.Kd6 Kf7. And this is example 1. With 5.Kd7 white wins the pawn and with it the game.
This is Example 4, but with the important difference that Black's is to move. With 1...Kc7, black has opposition. The white king does not enter: 2.Kb5 Kb7 3.Kc5 Kc7. Black holds a draw!

texts: The black king can no longer guard the pawn.
